claims.text: The ability of lightweight HEAs to combine low density, mechanical strength, corrosion resistance, and high-temperature oxidation resistance arises from synergistic lattice-distortion and sluggish-diffusion effects.
Lattice distortion and sluggish diffusion stabilize a single-phase solid solution.
Lattice distortion and sluggish diffusion inhibit the formation of detrimental intermetallic phases.
The initial lightweight HEA is in a single-phase solid-solution state.
Al, Mg, and Ti are examples of low-density constituent elements.
Compositional variations can systematically change lattice distortion while retaining the same phase structure.
Mechanical-strength and corrosion-resistance tests are to be conducted at room temperature.
Oxidation resistance is to be tested at an elevated temperature of approximately 800°C.
Lattice distortion produces atomic-scale strain fields.
Lattice distortion strengthens the alloy by impeding dislocation motion.
Sluggish diffusion reduces atomic mobility.
Reduced atomic mobility suppresses intermetallic-phase formation.
Intermetallic-phase formation can compromise corrosion resistance.
Intermetallic-phase formation can compromise high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Higher lattice distortion will increase mechanical strength relative to a minimally distorted baseline alloy.
Higher lattice distortion will improve corrosion resistance relative to a minimally distorted baseline alloy.
Higher lattice distortion will improve high-temperature oxidation resistance relative to a minimally distorted baseline alloy.
Above a critical lattice-distortion threshold, the alloy will become phase-unstable.
Excessive lattice distortion can lead to the formation of brittle intermetallic phases.
The quantitative relationship between lattice distortion and the combined target properties is not well established.
